title: Micro-Macro Coupled Koopman Modeling on Graph for Traffic Flow Prediction
one_liner: A unified model that predicts both how individual cars move and how traffic density changes by lifting the real nonlinear dynamics into a simpler linear space.
lead: Traffic has two sides that fight each other: what individual cars do (swerving, accelerating, changing lanes) and how the overall flow moves (congestion waves, smooth-flowing highways). Traditional models pick one side or the other. This paper shows how to model both at once by using a mathematical trick called Koopman lifting: translate the messy real-world motion into a high-dimensional space where the dynamics become linear and predictable, then translate predictions back.

paras: Microscopic models (focus on one car at a time) do a good job predicting what an individual driver will do next—turn left, speed up, stay put—because they learn from detailed car-by-car sequences. But they miss the forest: when lots of cars bunch together, they move as a wave, and that wave has rules the car-level model never learned, because the model sees each car in isolation and never learns how density and flow feedback into individual motion.

Macroscopic models (focus on the highway as a whole) capture the wave: they see traffic density (how crowded a stretch of road is) and predict how fast it will clear. But they flatten the picture—they lose the fact that a solo car is still a solo car, and a truck behaves differently than a motorcycle.
The worst part: older methods that try both require you to feed them long histories of past car positions. In real traffic, you often don't have that—you just have now.

callout.html: Koopman lifts microscopic and macroscopic dynamics into a shared linear space so a single model predicts both vehicle motion and flow evolution from the current state alone.

steps.text: Record current car positions and road-section densities.
Connect each car to nearby cars. Edges mean one car influences another.
Classify what each driver intends (speed up, slow, lane-change) from position alone, because intent determines which operator to apply next.
Transform car positions and densities into a high-dimensional linear view.
Apply a linear operator, then transform back to real positions and densities.

paras: Instead of separate models for cars and flow, MMCKM builds one operator that acts on a joint representation of both. The operator is linear in Koopman space, so it avoids the nonlinear prediction collapse that derails simpler models.

hidden.name: how much the dynamics become linear
paras: Real traffic motion is nonlinear: a car's next speed depends on the squared distance to the car ahead, densities interact in waves, and accidents create sudden jumps. A Koopman operator is a hidden transformation that maps this nonlinear world into a high-dimensional space where motion follows a simple linear rule (apply the same operator again and again). The paper measures this by checking whether predictions in Koopman space stay on track: if the lifted dynamics are truly linear, repeated applications of the operator should forecast accurately.

The paper estimates Koopman linearity by learning scenario-adaptive operators—different evolvers for different driving intents—so that each piece of the dynamics (aggressive driving, cautious driving, flow blockage) has its own linear rule. Better linearity means fewer steps where the prediction drifts, because a true linear rule can be applied over and over without accumulating error from nonlinear terms that were not captured in the model.

heat.caption: Darker means higher nonlinearity; braking and congestion zones are hardest to linearize.

reads.html: Koopman linearity is how accurately the same rule predicts the next step over and over. High linearity means a simple operator can forecast far ahead.

The paper learns scenario-adaptive Koopman evolvers, where each intent class (from the discriminator) has its own operator, and validates that repeated application of these operators forecasts vehicle trajectories and flow density with low error.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: Lifting to simplicity
paras: Traffic prediction fails at nonlinearity. A car moving 5 meters per second in bumper-to-bumper traffic responds differently than the same car moving 5 meters per second on an empty highway. The collision risk is not linear; it follows a curve. Densities don't add linearly either—a highway with half density does not move at half speed.

Koopman's trick: instead of modeling the real state space directly, map into a much higher-dimensional space where the observed dynamics are linear. Think of it like rotating your view: a spiraling tornado looks like a straight line if you rotate your viewpoint to face it head-on. Once in that space, a single linear operator (a set of rules that say: multiply each dimension by a specific number and add a specific offset) predicts the next step correctly. Apply it again for step two. This works because the high dimensions absorb the nonlinearity into the encoding itself.

The paper adds a second insight: traffic intent matters. A car that is about to brake is in a different regime than one about to accelerate. The Intent Discriminator (a small classifier that sees position and guesses intent) switches which Koopman operator applies. So instead of one global linear rule, there are several scenario-specific linear rules, and the right one is chosen in real time. This keeps the operator simple and keeps errors from compounding.

The coupling is explicit: each car's dynamics are influenced by overall flow density (a macro quantity pushed down to micro level), and density evolution is influenced by individual car motions (micro pushed up). In Koopman space, both feedback paths are embedded in the operator, so a single forward step captures both.

stages.s: Current car positions, densities, and observed intents
Transform to Koopman space (high-dim linear view)
Transform back to car positions and densities
Next positions and flow density for the next moment

math.words: For each intent i, the next state in Koopman space is the operator applied to the current state. The operator is a matrix that encodes both micro and macro evolution and their coupling.

items.html: If a car crashes or a lane closes, the nonlinear shock does not fit in any Koopman operator learned from normal traffic. The model predicts the continuation of the pre-crash trend, not the actual congestion wave.
If the intent discriminator misfires—guessing brake when the car is actually accelerating—it applies the wrong operator, and the forecast drifts immediately.
If nearby cars are not connected in the dynamic graph, their influence is not captured. A distant car in a separate cluster will be forecasted as if alone.
With good intent classification and a well-learned scenario-specific operators, the model forecasts many steps ahead without diverging, handling both car-level detail and flow-level patterns at once.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulator with 50–100 cars on a circular track. Record their starting positions and intended accelerations (fast, slow, medium). Now hide the intents and give the model only current positions and densities. Have it predict 20 steps ahead. Compare predicted positions to ground-truth positions. Separately, measure predicted density error (compare predicted number of cars per section to actual count). The demo must show: (1) prediction accuracy stays stable across all 20 steps (Koopman linearity holds), (2) density predictions track the actual flow waves (macro coupling works), and (3) no historical data was needed—only the snapshot at step 0.
demo.metric_eq: avg_position_error = mean(|predicted_car_i_x - actual_car_i_x| over all cars and all 20 steps); density_wave_mae = mean(|predicted_density_per_section - actual_density_per_section|); history_used = 0 frames.
demo.closing: A good demo must show that one model predicts both individual car positions and overall flow density accurately from only the current snapshot—something older methods could not do.
